Main.sentence: Stanley Ann Dunham (November 29, 1942 – November 7, 1995) was an American ___E:anthropologist U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthropology)___ who specialized in the ___E:economic anthropology U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economic_anthropology)___ and ___E:rural development U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rural_development)___ of Indonesia.

Born in ___E:Wichita, Kansas U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wichita,_Kansas)___ , she studied at the ___E:East–West Center U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East%E2%80%93West_Center)___ and at the ___E:University of Hawaiʻi at Mānoa U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Hawai%CA%BBi_at_M%C4%81noa)___ in ___E:Honolulu U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Honolulu)___ , where she earned a Bachelor of Arts (1967), a Master of Arts (1974), and a PhD (1992) in anthropology.

Drawing on her interest in craftsmanship, weaving, and the role of women in ___E:cottage industries U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cottage_industries)___ , Dunham conducted research on women's work on the island of ___E:Java U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Java)___ and blacksmithing in Indonesia.

To address the problem of poverty in rural villages, she designed ___E:microcredit U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Microcredit)___ programs while working as a consultant for the ___E:United States Agency for International Development U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Agency_for_International_Development)___ .

In ___E:Jakarta U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jakarta)___ , she worked for the ___E:Ford Foundation U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ford_Foundation)___ , and consulted for the ___E:Asian Development Bank U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asian_Development_Bank)___ in ___E:Pakistan U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pakistan)___ .

Towards the latter part of her life, she worked with ___E:Bank Rakyat Indonesia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_Rakyat_Indonesia)___ , where she helped apply her research to the largest ___E:microfinance U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Microfinance)___ program in the world.

As the mother of ___E:Barack Obama U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barack_Obama)___ , the ___E:44th president of the United States U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidency_of_Barack_Obama)___ , her anthropological research faced renewed interest after his election, with new symposiums, endowments, fellowships, exhibitions, and publications dedicated to reexamining her life and upholding her legacy.

Dunham was born on November 29, 1942, in ___E:Wichita, Kansas U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wichita,_Kansas)___ , the only child of ___E:Madelyn Lee Payne U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Madelyn_Dunham)___ and ___E:Stanley Armour Dunham U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanley_Armour_Dunham)___ .

She was of predominantly English ancestry, with small amounts of Scottish, Welsh, Irish, ___E:German U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_Americans)___ and Swiss-German.  ___E:Wild Bill Hickok U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wild_Bill_Hickok)___ was her sixth cousin, five times removed.  ___E:Ancestry.com U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancestry.com)___ claimed on July 30, 2012, after using a combination of old documents and ___E:yDNA U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/YDNA)___ analysis, that Dunham's mother was descended from ___E:John Punch U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Punch_(slave))___ , an African slave in seventeenth-century colonial ___E:Virginia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virginia)___ .

Her parents were born in Kansas and met in Wichita, where they married on May 5, 1940.  After the ___E:attack on Pearl Harbor U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Attack_on_Pearl_Harbor)___ , her father joined the ___E:United States Army U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Army)___ , and her mother worked at a ___E:Boeing U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boeing)___ plant in Wichita.
According to Dunham, she was named after her father because he wanted a son, though her relatives doubt this story.

Her maternal uncle recalled that her mother named Dunham after her favorite actress ___E:Bette Davis U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bette_Davis)___ ' character (Stanley Timberlake) in the film In This Our Life because she thought Stanley, as a girl's name, sounded sophisticated.
As a child and teenager, she was known as Stanley.

Other children teased her about her name. Nonetheless, she used it through high school, "apologizing for it each time she introduced herself in a new town."  By the time Dunham began attending college, she was known by her middle name, Ann, instead.

After ___E:World War II U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II)___ , Dunham's family moved from Wichita to ___E:California U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California)___ while her father attended the ___E:University of California, Berkeley U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_California,_Berkeley)___ .

In 1948, they moved to ___E:Ponca City, Oklahoma U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ponca_City,_Oklahoma)___ , and from there to ___E:Vernon, Texas U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vernon,_Texas)___ , and then to ___E:El Dorado, Kansas U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Dorado,_Kansas)___ .

In 1955, the family moved to ___E:Seattle U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seattle)___ , Washington, where her father was employed as a furniture salesman and her mother worked as vice president of a bank. They lived in an apartment complex in the ___E:Wedgwood U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wedgwood,_Seattle)___ neighborhood where she attended ___E:Nathan Eckstein Junior High School U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nathan_Eckstein_Middle_School)___ .

In 1957, Dunham's family moved to ___E:Mercer Island U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercer_Island)___ , an ___E:Eastside U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastside_(King_County,_Washington))___ suburb of Seattle.
Dunham's parents wanted their daughter to attend the newly opened ___E:Mercer Island High School U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercer_Island_High_School)___ .

At the school, teachers Val Foubert and Jim Wichterman taught the importance of challenging social norms and questioning authority to the young Dunham, and she took the lessons to heart: "She felt she didn't need to date or marry or have children." One classmate remembered her as "intellectually way more mature than we were and a little bit ahead of her time, in an off-center way",  and a high school friend described her as knowledgeable and progressive: "If you were concerned about something going wrong in the world, Stanley would know about it first.
We were liberals before we knew what liberals were." Another called her "the original feminist".
She went through high school "reading beatnik poets and French existentialists".
On August 21, 1959, ___E:Hawaii U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii)___ became the 50th state to be admitted into the Union.

Dunham's parents sought business opportunities in the new state, and after graduating from high school in 1960, Dunham and her family moved to ___E:Honolulu U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Honolulu)___ .
Dunham enrolled at the ___E:University of Hawaii at Mānoa U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Hawaii_at_Manoa)___ .

While attending a ___E:Russian language U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_language)___ class, Dunham met ___E:Barack Obama Sr. U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barack_Obama_Sr.)___ , the school's first African student.
Dunham and Obama Sr. were married on the Hawaiian island of ___E:Maui U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maui)___ on February 2, 1961, despite parental opposition from both families.
Dunham was three months pregnant.
Obama Sr. eventually informed Dunham about his first marriage in Kenya but claimed he was divorced.
Years later she discovered this was false.

Obama Sr.'s first wife, Kezia, later said she had granted her consent for him to marry a second wife in keeping with ___E:Luo U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luo_(Kenya_and_Tanzania)#Marriage_customs)___ customs.
On August 4, 1961, at the age of 18, Dunham gave birth to her first child, Barack Obama, in Honolulu.

Friends in the state of Washington recall her visiting with her month-old baby in 1961.   She studied at the ___E:University of Washington U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Washington)___ from September 1961 to June 1962, and lived as a single mother in the ___E:Capitol Hill U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capitol_Hill,_Seattle)___ neighborhood of Seattle with her son while her husband continued his studies in Hawaii.

When Obama Sr. graduated from the ___E:University of Hawaii U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Hawaii)___ in June 1962,  he left for ___E:Cambridge, Massachusetts U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cambridge,_Massachusetts)___ , where he began graduate study at ___E:Harvard University U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvard_University)___ in fall 1962.  Dunham returned to Honolulu and resumed her undergraduate education at the University of Hawaii with the spring semester in January 1963. During this time, her parents helped her raise her child.
Dunham filed for divorce in January 1964 and Obama Sr. did not contest.

At the ___E:East–West Center U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East%E2%80%93West_Center)___ , Dunham met ___E:Lolo Soetoro U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lolo_Soetoro)___ ,  a ___E:Javanese U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Javanese_people)___  surveyor who came to Honolulu in September 1962. In 1965, Soetoro and Dunham were married in Hawaii, and in 1966, Soetoro returned to ___E:Indonesia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indonesia)___ .

Dunham graduated from the University of Hawaii with a B.A. in anthropology on August 6, 1967, and moved in October the same year with her son to ___E:Jakarta U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jakarta)___ , Indonesia, to rejoin her husband.

The family first lived in a newly built neighborhood in the Menteng Dalam ___E:administrative village U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Administrative_Village_(Indonesia))___ of the ___E:Tebet U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tebet,_South_Jakarta)___ ___E:subdistrict U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subdistricts_of_Indonesia)___ in ___E:South Jakarta U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Jakarta)___ for two and a half years.

In 1970 they moved to the Matraman Dalam neighborhood in the Pegangsaan administrative village of the ___E:Menteng U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menteng)___ subdistrict in ___E:Central Jakarta U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Jakarta)___ .
On August 15, 1970, Soetoro and Dunham had a daughter, ___E:Maya Kassandra Soetoro U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maya_Soetoro-Ng)___ .

Dunham enriched her son's education with ___E:correspondence courses U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Correspondence_course)___ in English, recordings of ___E:Mahalia Jackson U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahalia_Jackson)___ , and speeches by ___E:Martin Luther King Jr. U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Luther_King_Jr.)___ In 1971, she sent Obama back to Hawaii to attend ___E:Punahou School U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punahou_School)___ .
In August 1972, Dunham and her daughter moved back to Hawaii so Dunham could begin graduate study in anthropology at the University of Hawaii at Manoa.

Dunham's graduate work was supported by an ___E:Asia Foundation U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Asia_Foundation)___ grant from August 1972 to July 1973 and by an East–West Center Technology and Development Institute grant from August 1973 to December 1978.

Dunham completed her coursework at the University of Hawaii for an M.A. in anthropology in December 1974.  She spent three years in Hawaii, then returned to Indonesia in 1975 with her daughter to do anthropological field work.   Lolo Soetoro and Dunham divorced on November 5, 1980; Lolo Soetoro married Erna Kustina in 1980 and had two children, a son, Yusuf Aji Soetoro (born 1981), and daughter, Rahayu Nurmaida Soetoro (born 1987).
Dunham was not estranged from either ex-husband and encouraged her children to feel connected to their fathers.

Dunham taught English in ___E:Central Jakarta U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Jakarta)___ from 1968 to 1972. She was also assistant director of the Indonesia-America Friendship Institute  and later a department head and director of the Institute of Management Education and Development.
During this same time, Dunham co-founded the Ganesha Volunteers (Indonesian Heritage Society) at the ___E:National Museum U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Museum_(Indonesia))___ in Jakarta.

She was also a crafts instructor in weaving, ___E:batik U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Batik)___ , and dye at the ___E:Bishop Museum U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernice_P._Bishop_Museum)___ in Honolulu from 1972 to 1975.

She worked in ___E:rural development U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rural_development)___ , championing women's work and ___E:microcredit U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Microcredit)___ for the world's poor with leaders from organizations supporting ___E:Indonesian human rights U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_rights_in_Indonesia)___ , ___E:women's rights U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women%27s_rights_in_Indonesia)___ , and grass-roots ___E:development U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economic_history_of_Indonesia)___ .

In March 1977, under the supervision of agricultural economics professor Leon A. Mears, she developed and taught a short lecture course at the Faculty of Economics of the ___E:University of Indonesia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Indonesia)___ (FEUI) in Jakarta for staff members of the ___E:Indonesian National Development Planning Agency U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ministry_of_National_Development_Planning_of_Indonesia)___ .

She was a short-term consultant in the office of the ___E:International Labour Organization U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Labour_Organization)___ (ILO) in Jakarta, writing recommendations on village industries and other non-agricultural enterprises for the Indonesian government's third five-year development plan (REPELITA III) between May and June 1978.   Dunham worked as a rural industries consultant in Central Java on the ___E:Indonesian Ministry of Industry U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ministry_of_Industry_(Indonesia))___ 's Provincial Development Program (PDP I) from October 1978 to December 1980. The program was funded by the ___E:USAID U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Agency_for_International_Development)___ and implemented through ___E:Development Alternatives, Inc. U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Development_Alternatives_Incorporated)___ (DAI).

Dunham was the program officer for women and employment in the ___E:Ford Foundation U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ford_Foundation)___ 's Southeast Asia regional office in Jakarta from January 1981 to November 1984.   While at the Ford Foundation, she developed a model of ___E:microfinance U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Microfinance)___ which is now the standard in Indonesia, a country that is a world leader in micro-credit systems.

Peter Geithner, father of ___E:Tim Geithner U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tim_Geithner)___ (who later became ___E:U.S. Secretary of the Treasury U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_the_Treasury)___ in her son's administration), was head of the foundation's Asia grant-making at that time.

From May to November 1986 and from August to November 1987, Dunham was a cottage industries development consultant for the ___E:Agricultural Development Bank of Pakistan U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zarai_Taraqiati_Bank_Limited)___ (ADBP) under the Gujranwala Integrated Rural Development Project (GADP).

The credit component of the project was implemented in the ___E:Gujranwala U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gujranwala_District)___ district of the ___E:Punjab U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punjab,_Pakistan)___ province of ___E:Pakistan U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pakistan)___ with funding from the ___E:Asian Development Bank U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asian_Development_Bank)___ and ___E:IFAD U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Fund_for_Agricultural_Development)___ , with the credit component implemented through ___E:Louis Berger International, Inc U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Berger_Group)___ .
Dunham worked closely with the ___E:Lahore U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lahore)___ office of the Punjab Small Industries Corporation (PSIC).

From January 1988 to 1995, Dunham was a consultant and research coordinator for Indonesia's oldest bank, ___E:Bank Rakyat Indonesia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_Rakyat_Indonesia)___ (BRI) in Jakarta, with her work funded by USAID and the ___E:World Bank U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Bank)___ .

In March 1993, Dunham was a research and policy coordinator for ___E:Women's World Banking U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women%27s_World_Banking)___ (WWB) in New York.  She helped WWB manage the Expert Group Meeting on Women and Finance in New York in January 1994, and helped the WWB take prominent roles in the UN's ___E:Fourth World Conference on Women U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourth_World_Conference_on_Women)___ held September 4–15, 1995 in ___E:Beijing U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beijing)___ , and in the UN regional conferences and NGO forums that preceded it.

Dunham carried out research on village industries in the ___E:Yogyakarta Special Region U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special_Region_of_Yogyakarta)___ within ___E:Central Java U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Java)___ in Indonesia under a student grant from the East–West Center from June 1977 through September 1978.  As a ___E:weaver U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weaving)___ herself, Dunham was interested in village industries, and moved to ___E:Yogyakarta City U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yogyakarta_(city))___ , the center of ___E:Javanese U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Java)___ ___E:handicrafts U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Handicrafts)___ .

Dunham was awarded a ___E:PhD U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PhD)___ in ___E:anthropology U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthropology)___ from the University of Hawaii on August 9, 1992. Her 1,043-page dissertation was completed under the supervision of ___E:Alice G. Dewey U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alice_G._Dewey)___ .

Titled Peasant blacksmithing in Indonesia: Surviving against all odds ,  it was described by anthropologist Michael Dove as "a classic, in-depth, on-the-ground anthropological study of a 1,200-year-old industry".

According to Dove, Dunham's dissertation challenged popular perceptions regarding economically and politically marginalized groups, and countered the notions that the roots of poverty lie with the poor themselves and that cultural differences are responsible for the gap between less-developed countries and the industrialized West.

___E:Duke University Press U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duke_University_Press)___ published a new version of Dunham's dissertation as a book in December 2009. It was revised and edited by Dunham's graduate advisor ___E:Alice G. Dewey U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alice_G._Dewey)___ and Nancy I. Cooper, with a foreword by Dunham's daughter, ___E:Maya Soetoro-Ng U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maya_Soetoro-Ng)___ .

In his afterword, ___E:Boston University U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston_University)___ anthropologist Robert W. Hefner describes Dunham's research as "prescient" and her legacy as "relevant today for anthropology, Indonesian studies, and engaged scholarship".

The book was launched at the 2009 annual meeting of the ___E:American Anthropological Association U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Anthropological_Association)___ in Philadelphia with a special Presidential Panel on Dunham's work; the 2009 meeting was taped by ___E:C-SPAN U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C-SPAN)___ .

Dunham produced a large amount of professional papers that are held in collections of the ___E:National Anthropological Archives U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Anthropological_Archives)___ (NAA).
Her daughter donated a collection of them that is categorized as the S. Ann Dunham papers, 1965–2013 .

This collection contains case studies, correspondence, field notebooks, lectures, photographs, reports, research files, research proposals, surveys, and floppy disks documenting her dissertation research on blacksmithing, as well as her professional work as a consultant for organizations such as the Ford Foundation and the Bank Rakyat Indonesia (BRI).
They are housed at the ___E:Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smithsonian_National_Museum_of_Natural_History)___ .

Her field notes have been digitized and, in 2020, ___E:Smithsonian Magazine U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smithsonian_Magazine)___ noted that an effort had been established for a project to transcribe them.
In late 1994, Dunham was living and working in Indonesia.
One night, during dinner at a friend's house in Jakarta, she experienced stomach pain. A visit to a local physician led to an initial diagnosis of indigestion.

Dunham returned to the United States in early 1995 and was examined at the ___E:Memorial Sloan–Kettering Cancer Center U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Memorial_Sloan%E2%80%93Kettering_Cancer_Center)___ in New York City and diagnosed with ___E:uterine cancer U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uterine_cancer)___ .
By this time, the cancer had spread to her ovaries.
She moved back to Hawaii to live near her widowed mother and died on November 7, 1995, 22 days short of her 53rd birthday.

Following a memorial service at the University of Hawaii, Obama and his sister spread their mother's ashes in the Pacific Ocean at ___E:Lanai Lookout U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Koko_Head)___ on the south side of ___E:Oahu U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oahu)___ .
Obama scattered the ashes of his grandmother ___E:Madelyn Dunham U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Madelyn_Dunham)___ in the same spot on December 23, 2008, weeks after his election to the presidency.
Obama talked about Dunham's death in a 30-second campaign advertisement ("Mother") arguing for health care reform.
The ad featured a photograph of Dunham holding a young Obama in her arms as Obama talks about her last days worrying about expensive medical bills.
The topic also came up in a 2007 speech in ___E:Santa Barbara U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Barbara,_California)___ .

Dunham's employer-provided health insurance covered most of the costs of her medical treatment, leaving her to pay the deductible and uncovered expenses, which came to several hundred dollars per month.

Her employer-provided disability insurance denied her claims for uncovered expenses because the insurance company said her cancer was a ___E:preexisting condition U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Preexisting_condition)___ .

She felt that somehow, wandering through uncharted territory, we might stumble upon something that will, in an instant, seem to represent who we are at the core. That was very much her philosophy of life — to not be limited by fear or narrow definitions, to not build walls around ourselves and to do our best to find kinship and beauty in unexpected places.
In his 1995 memoir Dreams from My Father , Barack Obama wrote, "My mother's confidence in needlepoint virtues depended on a faith I didn't possess...

In a land [Indonesia] where fatalism remained a necessary tool for enduring hardship ... she was a lonely witness for ___E:secular humanism U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secular_humanism)___ , a soldier for ___E:New Deal U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Deal)___ , ___E:Peace Corps U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peace_Corps)___ , position-paper liberalism."  In his 2006 book The Audacity of Hope Obama wrote, "I was not raised in a religious household ...
My mother's own experiences ... only reinforced this inherited skepticism.
Her memories of the Christians who populated her youth were not fond ones ...

And yet for all her professed secularism, my mother was in many ways the most spiritually awakened person that I've ever known."  "Religion for her was "just one of the many ways—and not necessarily the best way—that man attempted to control the unknowable and understand the deeper truths about our lives," Obama wrote.
Maxine Box, Dunham's best friend in high school, recalled that Dunham openly identified as an atheist and was intellectually engaged with the topic and other subjects well in advance of her peers.
On the other hand, Dunham's daughter, Maya Soetoro-Ng, when asked later if her mother was an atheist, said, "I wouldn't have called her an atheist.
She was an agnostic.

She basically gave us all the good books—the Bible, the Hindu Upanishads and the ___E:Buddhist scripture U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buddhist_texts)___ , the Tao Te Ching —and wanted us to recognize that everyone has something beautiful to contribute."  "Jesus, she felt, was a wonderful example.
But she felt that a lot of Christians behaved in un-Christian ways."
In a 2007 speech, Obama contrasted the beliefs of his mother to those of her parents, and commented both on her spirituality and her skepticism.
He described his mother's parents as coming from a Baptist and Methodist background in a culture that was nonobservant and skeptical of organized religion.
Obama, who identifies as a Christian, also had a father from a Kenyan Muslim family who was not religious and did not practice Islam.

The ___E:University of Hawaii at Mānoa U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Hawaii_at_Manoa)___ (UH) first held a symposium about Dunham in September 2008.  The University of Hawaii Foundation established the Ann Dunham Soetoro Endowment, which supports a faculty position housed in the Anthropology Department at UH, and the Ann Dunham Soetoro Graduate Fellowships, which provide funding for students associated with the ___E:East–West Center U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East%E2%80%93West_Center)___ (EWC).

Dunham's alma mater, Mercer Island High School, began offering the Stanley Ann Dunham Scholarship in 2010.  President Obama and his family visited an exhibition of his mother's anthropological work on display at the EWC in 2012.

An exhibition of Dunham's Javanese ___E:batik U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Batik)___ textile collection ( A Lady Found a Culture in its Cloth: Barack Obama's Mother and Indonesian Batiks ) toured six museums in the United States, finishing the tour at the ___E:Textile Museum U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Textile_Museum_(Washington,_D.C.))___ of Washington, D.C., in August 2009.  Earlier in her life, Dunham was interested in the textile arts as a weaver, creating wall hangings for her own enjoyment.
After moving to Indonesia, she was attracted to the striking textile art of the batik and began to collect a variety of different fabrics.

Dunham was awarded the ___E:Bintang Jasa U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orders,_decorations,_and_medals_of_Indonesia#Bintang_Jasa_.28.22Bravery_Star_Decoration.22.29)___ Utama, ___E:Indonesia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indonesia)___ 's highest civilian award, in December 2010; the Bintang Jasa is awarded at three levels, and is presented to those individuals who have made notable civic and cultural contributions.

A major biography of Dunham by former New York Times reporter Janny Scott, titled A Singular Woman , was published in 2011.  Filmmaker Vivian Norris's feature length biographical film of Ann Dunham entitled Obama Mama (La mère d'Obama-French title) premiered on May 31, 2014, as part of the 40th annual Seattle International Film Festival, not far from where Dunham grew up on Mercer Island.
